As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece around 4000-5000 years ago. These early cultures recognized the stars and constellations, and some even believed in the existence of a divine realm beyond the Earth.

The idea that space was a void of darkness illuminated only by stars and galaxies developed over time as our understanding of the universe evolved. The ancient Greeks, for example, believed in a geocentric model of the universe, where the Earth was at the center and the stars and planets orbited around it. However, as early as the 5th century BCE, the Greek philosopher Democritus proposed a heliocentric model, where the Sun was at the center of the solar system.

The modern understanding of outer space as a vast, dark expanse of stars and galaxies began to take shape during the Renaissance and the Scientific Revolution of the 16th and 17th centuries. The invention of the telescope by Galileo Galilei in 1608 allowed for the observation of the night sky in greater detail, revealing the existence of moons, planets, and other celestial bodies beyond the Earth.

The concept of space as a blue-colored void was likely a result of the Earth's atmosphere scattering sunlight, giving the sky its blue appearance. This idea was first proposed by the English scientist Isaac Newton in the 17th century, who described the Earth's atmosphere as a "blue-colored" medium that scattered sunlight.

However, it wasn't until the 20th century that the concept of space as a vast, dark expanse of stars and galaxies became widely accepted. The discovery of the first galaxy, Andromeda, in 1923 by the American astronomer Edwin Hubble, marked a major milestone in our understanding of the universe. Since then, numerous space missions and observations have revealed the existence of billions of galaxies, stars, and other celestial objects, transforming our understanding of the universe and its place in the cosmos.
